title: Introducing tsrs: A port of TypeScript to Rust
excerpt: Cloudflare and VoidZero are now working with Max Schwenk of Owner.com on tsrs , a Rust port of the TypeScript compiler. We are doing this work in close collaboration with the TypeScript team, and incubating tsrs as part of the Oxc JavaScript compiler toolchain . Our goal is to help developers spend less time waiting for their code to be checked and more time building. Making TypeScript faster and more memory-efficient also helps bring complete development environments to more places, including right in your browser. To be clear, we are not forking TypeScript. We believe the TypeScript team should remain in full control of the language’s design and direction. They have maintained a long-term vision while guiding TypeScript’s adoption across the JavaScript community. We do not want to change that. The TypeScript team can move quite fast on many things, but for some features they may spend years intentionally exploring options and making prototypes before picking the right implementation. A Rust port has to follow those decisions closely, or it will eventually fall apart and become incompatible. We have to preserve the TypeScript language strictly based on its original implementation – and the TypeScript team should remain solely responsible for deciding what that looks like. Performance and memory improvements Early benchmarks of our Rust port of TypeScript are promising: tsrs is up to 8x faster and uses ~70% less memory compared to TypeScript 7.0 when using the same number of type check workers: As you can see, the next version of TypeScript already brings many performance improvements, making TypeScript 7.1 beta up to 2.5x faster than TypeScript 7.0. Some of these optimizations were upstreamed from tsrs , and we’re hoping to find more. You may have seen recent benchmarks of different TypeScript ports with various performance claims, often due to using larger machine types and different options compared to TypeScript’s defaults. We worked with the TypeScript team to ensure the above benchmarks are comparing the same configuration. By default, tsrs ships with an adaptive configuration dependent on the machine type that uses more memory but is even faster: Try tsrs TypeScript in Rust aims to be a faithful port of TypeScript. You can try an experimental release by installing the tsrs package from npm: npm install tsrs npx tsrs Why now? We’ve seen many attempts at porting TypeScript to other languages over the years. Because of the complexity involved, only one of the ports succeeded: the TypeScript team’s port of TypeScript from JavaScript to Go. However, frontier AI models can now do large-scale ports almost independently in a matter of days. We have now seen slopforks, faithful ports, and completely re-architected versions of TypeScript in Rust or C++. There is clearly a demand for even faster TypeScript. Why Rust? You might be thinking: “TypeScript’s Go port already made TypeScript 10x faster and far more memory efficient than the previous version written in TypeScript. Why isn’t that enough?” However, it’s not just about speed. Rust offers some unique advantages: running in WebAssembly . The Rust + Wasm story has always been strong, and one of the reasons comes down to the fundamentals of Rust’s language design. When you compile a Go program to Wasm, you have to compile Go’s garbage collector along with it. But Rust’s memory management model enables straightforward memory interactions between a WebAssembly guest and host. This is one of the key things that makes Rust a much better fit for the WebAssembly use-case: memory efficiency. Cloudflare Workers have supported Wasm for a long time. Just a few weeks ago we announced supporting native Rust in Workers with the new Emscripten target for wasm-bindgen. When you run entire software build and deployment systems in tight loops on Workers, the benefits of a small memory footprint pay off quickly. It means you can run these workloads so efficiently that it’s now possible to run ful

title: 8 eMudhra certificates are compromised. Here's what you need to know
excerpt: On October 19, 2026, at approximately 17:00 UTC, Cloudflare became aware that private keys associated with eight eMudhra intermediate certificates were compromised. These certificates were widely trusted by browsers, operating systems, and also within Cloudflare. Because the keys themselves are weak, an attacker can create a forged certificate for any domain and use it to impersonate servers to intercept or modify traffic. This is a serious security incident with implications across the Internet. For reference, here is a link to more information about how SSL certificates work and why they are so critical to the operation of the Internet. We immediately prioritized patching critical services across Cloudflare to protect our customers ahead of the public disclosure of the vulnerability. Our security review has not identified active exploitation of this issue on Cloudflare services. We have released updates for the Cloudflare One Clients, also known as WARP or the 1.1.1.1 app, and Cloudflare Tunnel, also known as cloudflared. We have also deployed mitigations across our CDN, Developer, and Zero Trust products. If you are using Cloudflare Zero Trust with Gateway and an up-to-date client (see below), you are automatically protected. Our response We prioritized updating services that use public certificates to authenticate remote endpoints, including proxies connecting to origins and applications calling external APIs. In parallel, we updated shared trust stores, base images, and other shared foundations, providing a common mitigation path for services that inherit their certificate trust from those sources. We paired these updates with reloads, restarts, and image deployments needed to activate them. Applications with bundled or custom trust stores received separate assessment and updates. This work addresses certificate-based authentication, not a weakness in TLS’s encryption algorithms. Teams across Cloudflare are presently working on further remediation. We are making progress, but there's much work still to be done. Some customers will need to take action on software or trust configurations that they operate, especially on their origin servers. The recommended actions are summarized below. What customers should do Developer guidance For developers, look beneath the SDK. An API client may delegate certificate verification to an HTTP library, a language runtime, the operating system, or a custom trust configuration. Updating the SDK alone may not change the underlying policy. Once you patch, you may notice certificate errors in your dashboards. It's important to not resolve these errors by disabling verification. That would remove the authentication protection these updates are intended to restore. This incident affects many software stacks that rely on the WebPKI for authentication. Mozilla’s Dennis Jackson has crowdsourced a list of commonly used packages that have been patched. We advise readers to upgrade as soon as possible. (Note that some of these may be indirect dependencies of your software stack, so look at the dependency tree.) Apply the relevant dependency updates, rebuild affected images, and confirm whether applications require a reload, restart, or redeployment. Dennis Jackson’s test site provides browser checks, non-browser testing instructions, and package update information. Results apply to the verification path being tested, not every application on the device. Validate through the application’s actual TLS path. A successful browser test does not prove that a background service is protected. Neither does a curl test if the application uses a different verifier. Timeline The timeline of events so far is below. Date and Time Event October 19, approximately 17:00 UTC Cloudflare becomes aware of the compromise and begins assessment. October 20, 02:00 UTC Cloudflare One Client and WARP app security updates published across platforms. October 20 09:15 UTC Cloudflare Tunnel (cloudflared) security update published. O

title: Introducing Amazon ECS Gateway: A fully-managed ingress solution for ECS services
excerpt: When platform teams manage containerized applications at scale on Amazon Elastic Container Service (Amazon ECS) , configuring ingress networking for each service often becomes a bottleneck. For every new service, teams must provision and connect Application Load Balancers (ALBs) , AWS Certificate Manager (ACM) certificates, AWS WAF web ACLs, and security groups, then keep those resources in sync as services scale, update, or operate. This per-service overhead slows down deployment velocity and increases the risk of configuration drift across an organization. Today, we’re announcing Amazon ECS Gateway , a new account-level resource that simplifies ingress networking for containerized workloads by dynamically provisioning and managing the necessary infrastructure on your behalf, with all resources created directly in your account. ECS Gateway introduces a clear separation of responsibilities between platform teams and application teams. Platform teams create and configure a gateway, defining organizational networking standards including subnets, security groups, TLS certificates, listener settings, and WAF web ACLs, in a single place. They then associate the gateway with one or more ECS clusters, making it available to services running on those clusters. Application teams opt their services in by adding a gateway connector parameter when creating or updating a service. ECS provisions the required per-service resources automatically: an ACM certificate, a unique DNS hostname, listener rules, target groups, and a service security group that permits inbound traffic only from the ALB. No networking expertise required. ECS Gateway offers host-based routing using ALBs and enables up to 25 services to share a single ALB, optimizing infrastructure costs. ECS manages the full lifecycle of the underlying infrastructure, provisioning the first ALB when your first service connects, adding more ALBs as capacity is reached, and removing them when no longer needed. Each service receives a unique DNS hostname, giving your teams a ready-to-use endpoint the moment provisioning completes. A first look at ECS Gateway In the ECS console , platform team can create a gateway and sets its configuration. The infrastructure role is an IAM role that ECS assumes to provision and manage networking resources such as ALBs, security groups, and certificates in your account. To create a gateway, provide a gateway name and select an infrastructure role. You can optionally associate the gateway with ECS clusters during creation or later. Choose a load balancing scheme, either public or VPC-internal traffic routing. Under Additional Settings , you can also set up a listener, port, maximum count of load balancers the gateway can scale to, and a web ACL lets you protect your web applications. Some settings, including the name, scheme, VPC, subnets, IP address type, listener protocol and port cannot be changed after gateway creation. Using AWS Command Line Interface (AWS CLI) , call CreateGateway with a name (unique per account), an infrastructure role, and a configuration object. No infrastructure is provisioned until a service connects with a gateway connector. aws ecs create-gateway \ --name my-team-gateway \ --infrastructure-role-arn arn:aws:iam::123456789012:role/ECSGatewayRole \ --configuration '{ "HostSharedAlb": { "networkConfiguration": { "subnets": [ "subnet-080779f9bd887757a", "subnet-03d5b2fead6bc6258", "subnet-0861210a397d31252", "subnet-06539e194023cb77a" ], "ipAddressType": "ipv4" }, "scheme": "internet-facing" } }' Once the gateway is created, you can take a look at the detailed configuration, gateway routes, load balancers, and associated clusters. Now associate the gateway with one or more clusters (many-to-many), to make it available to ECS services on those clusters. Use AssociateGatewayWithCluster to make the gateway available to services on a cluster: aws ecs associate-gateway-with-cluster \ --gateway my-team-gateway \ --cluster arn:aws:ecs:us-e

title: Making every harness durable
excerpt: Developers are familiar with running coding agents locally through harnesses like Pi, Claude Code, and others. They are reliable daily drivers for generating code, but keeping agents running around the clock requires your computer to be on and awake, which led to the laptop lid memes and Mac mini demand spike. Running harnesses in the cloud Harness workloads are moving to the cloud. Individual developers are deploying always-on coding agent workflows, projects like OpenWork and HanaAgent use open-source harnesses as the engines behind the apps, and engineers are building their own harness products. These harnesses are designed for long-lived processes that keep the session in memory, and agent tasks commonly run for minutes or hours. Locally, a harness has direct, continuous access to the workspace and session history on the same disk, so resuming interrupted work only requires a simple prompt. In the cloud, you can replicate that setup with a VM and persistent storage, but the VM doesn't automatically record which model and tool calls completed or resume interrupted turns after a crash. A failed turn or network error means lost work. Also, not every agent task executed through a harness needs a sandbox. Database queries and API calls can run securely in functions, and that also means required credentials never have to enter the sandbox. Making every harness durable We built eve and fx to run durably in the cloud out of the box, and today we are introducing durable-harness , which extends that durability to any harness, including Pi , OpenCode , Codex , and Claude Code . It uses the same machinery that powers Workflow SDK to survive crashes and function timeouts. With durable-harness , you can: Run any of these harnesses durably on Vercel Self-host a harness with your own Postgres instance Make your local harness workflow durable Build your own durable harness Sessions that survive a crash mid-turn Take the example of a coding agent adding a pricing page to an existing app. The agent reads the existing page, writes a new one, opens a pull request, and waits for CI to finish before reporting back. What happens if its function times out while CI is still running? Kill the function or drop the connection in the demo below to compare how the two agents recover and which work is repeated. Without durability, the agent stops work until it is manually restarted, and completed work is repeated unnecessarily. With durable-harness , a new function reads completed results from the log and resumes the turn. If the browser disconnects, the agent keeps running, and reconnecting catches up from the log. Logs and queues durable-harness is the newest package in our open source portfolio. It’s a set of adapters and utilities that let the harnesses you already use keep their sessions in a World , the Workflow SDK’s durable backend. It writes each step of a turn to a durable log. Before a model call or tool call runs, it records an intent, and when the call finishes, it records the outcome. The turn itself is backstopped with a queue message, so if its function dies, the queue hands the turn to a new function that reads the log and continues where it left off. After a crash, the log says what finished, what was running, and what never started: Completed calls never run again because their results are read from the log, so you’re never billed twice for a finished model call’s tokens. Models remember their previous calls rather than repeating them. Interrupted tools marked replay: 'safe' run again. Any other tool comes back to the model as possibly run, and the model decides whether to check. Harnesses that keep their own session files, like Claude Code's transcript, Codex's rollout, and OpenCode's event store, have every record mirrored into the log, so a new function or Sandbox rebuilds them from it. Pick your harness fx and eve are durable on their own. For the rest, durable-harness adds durability from the outside, without changing the harness.

title: Introducing ModuleLens: Zooming into PyTorch Modules for Human and Agentic Engineering
excerpt: Lida Li, Sr. Staff Software Engineer, Product ML Infra Introduction Modern recommendation systems, including those used for ads ranking and content discovery, have grown substantially in scale and complexity. This growth stems from both increasingly large model architectures. The resulting memory footprint often exceeds the capacity of a single GPU, making it necessary to shard production models across multiple GPUs using distributed training techniques such as Distributed Model Parallelism (DMP). This evolution brings challenges to the everyday engineer work on testing and debugging the model code. The bottleneck includes: Local Machine Hardware Limits : Because production models require multi-GPU setups, initializing a full model locally on a single-gpu workstation is virtually impossible. Input Data Dependencies : When an engineer modifies code inside a specific downstream module, getting realistic input data is a major hurdle. Traditionally, obtaining that input requires initializing the entire multi-GPU pipeline from scratch and executing every preceding module in the network — wasting immense amounts of time and computation resources. Slow Iteration Feedback Loops : Engineers face prolonged iteration loops when attempting to verify sub-module changes, as every code edit requires re-executing or re-initializing heavy distributed trainer setups. To eliminate these bottlenecks, we build ModuleLens , which pivots from a legacy “Model-First” paradigm to an isolated “Module-First” engineering framework. The following table contrasts these two operational paradigms across key engineering metrics: Under the module-first paradigm, engineers can isolate any given module, avoid multi-GPU model initialization entirely, and reconstruct and profile it locally within seconds. In addition to accelerating developer workflows, this modular foundation offers a fast, structured execution environment that empowers autonomous AI agents to analyze, refactor, and optimize PyTorch code independently. Architecture The architecture of ModuleLens is organized into three primary components: ModuleTracer for capturing runtime data, Module Repo for central storage, and a Consumption Layer serving human interfaces and AI-based tooling. The following diagram depicts this structure. ModuleTracer ModuleTracer is designed to capture and record all essential data — including input and output tensors, model parameter weights, and initialization arguments. This comprehensive tracking allows any target PyTorch module to be reconstructed seamlessly within the consumption layer, enabling offline execution with captured inputs and validation against expected outputs. To carry out trace capture, ModuleTracer relies on several key mechanisms: Non-Intrusive PyTorch Forward Hooks: Attaches listeners directly to PyTorch modules to seamlessly log parameter weights (state_dict), input and output tensors, and execution metadata during runtime. In-Memory Module Init Tracking: Ensures target modules can be reconstructed by dynamically tracking initialization arguments (__init__ args and kwargs). It achieves this in memory by inspecting imported classes and patching Python’s __import__ function. Resource-Efficient Tracing Loops: Reduces GPU compute overhead by registering early_stop_func and post_train_step_func callbacks. These wait for model warmup, capture data across a single training step, and terminate early. Optimized Handling of Large Tensors: To efficiently profile large tensors, ModuleTracer automatically enables shape-only tracing (log_shapes), logging solely tensor dimensions so that synthetic inputs can be reconstructed during restoration. Additionally, if an input tensor is shared across multiple modules, ModuleTracer retains only a single copy and uses reference links for all other instances. title: The Thin Orchestrator: How We Made Our AI Agents More Reliable by Giving the Router Less to Do
excerpt: Sometimes, giving an AI agent all of the knowledge it needs is the wrong approach. At Meta, we’ve seen notable improvements in efficiency and accuracy by keeping the orchestration layer of our data pipeline agents deliberately thin: It routes work and enforces reliability checks, while specialized agents do the domain reasoning. We’re sharing our own process and insights, plus how any team can apply this to their production AI agents. We built a 1,300-line orchestrator that routes 20+ workflows to 14 specialized AI agents. It performs zero domain work itself. That’s the point. When we first deployed AI agents to automate data column onboarding across Meta’s recommendation systems — a process spanning three code repositories, three programming languages, and up to six pipeline stages that must stay in sync — we did what most teams do: We built one smart agent that knew everything. It worked in demos. In production, it started hallucinating. The fix wasn’t better prompts or a bigger context window. It was giving the central agent less to do. We call this the thin orchestrator pattern: a router that owns sequencing and reliability checks, and leaves every domain decision to specialists. The Problem: More Context, Worse Results Our pipeline is config-as-code: Python configurations drive C++ code generation, which feeds data processing services, which populate analytics systems. Onboarding a single data column requires coordinated changes across configuration registries, backend services, and data pipelines, and each column moves through up to six stages before its data arrives. Our first approach was a single AI agent loaded with all domain knowledge, configuration schemas, code generation rules, pipeline routing logic, validation requirements, and population patterns for 10+ data sources. The agent had everything it needed. That was the problem. Past a certain context threshold, additional knowledge degraded rather than improved performance. The agent would cross-contaminate concepts, applying field naming conventions from one subsystem to another, or using a code generation pattern meant for one data source when populating from a different one. A preprint from the Windreich Department of Artificial Intelligence and Human Health at Mount Sinai found that orchestrated multiagent systems held 65.3% accuracy at 80-task batches where single agents fell to 16.6%, while reducing token usage up to 65-fold. The authors attribute this to the design’s isolation of tasks, which prevented context interference. We were experiencing the inverse, a single agent drowning in its own knowledge. We also evaluated an alternative single-agent approach. Its success rate was 70-80% with manual prompt engineering per task: An engineer had to craft a custom system prompt for each specific job. Without that handholding, success dropped to 10-20%. This wasn’t a prompt engineering problem. It was an architectural one. The Approach: A Thin Router With Specialist Workers We split the system into two layers: A deterministic orchestrator that performs zero domain work. It classifies intent, gathers required fields, runs reliability checks, and delegates to the right specialist. It never reasons about code, never generates configurations, and never touches the codebase. It’s a router. Fourteen specialized subagents , each a complete domain expert with isolated context. A schema management agent knows configuration registries. A population agent knows how to generate code for each of 10 data sources. A validation agent knows build systems and quality checks. No agent sees the full picture. That’s the feature, not the bug. The orchestrator follows a fixed 7-step protocol for every request: Read the relevant subagent’s instruction file. Check if the target already exists (prevent duplicates). Gather required fields from the user. Auto-discover what can be inferred (repository type, existing configurations). Reliability gate check for active warnings or required rev

title: GenRecs Tokenization: Transforming Ads Recommendation at Meta with Stable Model Vocabulary
excerpt: Generative Recommenders (GenRecs) represent a paradigm shift from scoring every ad to reasoning about ad content and user preferences together in order to predict the best outcome for advertisers. Leveraging the world knowledge built into LLMs makes ad matching more intelligent and precise, compounding gains for advertisers. GenRecs Tokenization is the foundational data representation that makes this possible. Rather than maintaining a dedicated ID for every item, GenRecs Tokenization represents each item with a set of tokens from a stable semantic vocabulary. Paired with Meta’s Generative Ads Model (GEM) and Meta’s Adaptive Ranking Model , GenRecs Tokenization has delivered a +0.35% lift in conversions across surfaces for advertisers. GenRecs improves the way Meta’s ads recommendation systems make predictions today. Short for Generative Recommenders , GenRecs shifts our approach from scoring every individual ad candidate to leveraging LLM architecture to deeply reason about ad content and user preferences simultaneously. By pairing pre-trained world knowledge with a semantic understanding of what an ad actually represents, the system moves beyond click-pattern matching to understand underlying user preferences. This allows the model to predict the most relevant ad for each person, even when surfacing brand-new products with no past product, ad or company engagement history. GenRecs Tokenization is the foundational data representation that makes this possible. Instead of maintaining a dedicated ID for every concept in the world, language models compose a small vocabulary of semantic tokens to represent any concept. Because tokens describe what an item (e.g., ads, products, services, etc.) is, the model can relate an item it has never seen engagement for, to items it knows well. A newly launched “trail shoe” inherits what the model has already learned about that category, rather than starting a new representation with no signal. GenRecs Tokenization introduces a structured vocabulary approach for ad recommendations, enabling GenRecs for both retrieval and ranking across every item type in the system, including ads, products, pages, and pixels. Meta’s state-of-the-art ads recommendation system drives ongoing advertiser performance improvements by learning about individual items and how they perform . LLMs present a unique opportunity to further improve the performance of recommendation systems by leveraging semantic tokenization in several ads use cases: Accelerating learning from new entities: Semantic tokenization helps models to infer relevance and establish relationships through shared concepts. New entities include newly created ads, niche products, and pages with limited engagement. Enabling cross-campaign transfer: Semantic tokenization creates a stable vocabulary that allows the models to carry insights across campaigns for advertisers. LLM scaling benefits: Semantic tokenization allows the benefits to compound with the LLM scaling curve’s improving performance. Infusing world knowledge: Semantic tokenization gives pre-trained language models a direct interface to reason about ad content and user intent. Once items are migrated to semantic tokens, models learn from token patterns much like LLMs do. In production, this yields: Prediction accuracy improvements in production: Paired with Meta’s GEM and Adaptive Ranking Model , GenRecs Tokenization delivered a +0.35% lift 1 in conversions. Compounding feedback loop: Better tail predictions yield better lessons from tail ads which enrich the training data to further improve predictions for all ads from the model, creating a performance improving feedback loop. A new way to scale: Across production ranking and retrieval, tokens bend the scaling curve along sequence length, training data, and model architecture. 1 Meta Internal Data, measured in February 2026. title: Inside Prometheus: Meta’s Journey to a Gigawatt-Scale Supercluster
excerpt: With the recent release of the Muse family of foundational models, we want to take you inside the infrastructure that has made it all possible. The first phase of Prometheus, our gigawatt-scale supercluster, is already complete and we’re working toward scaling it to comprise ~1 million GPUs. Prometheus also features technologies like closed-loop liquid cooling to help it operate efficiently. Right now, in New Albany, Ohio, Meta is undertaking its most ambitious AI infrastructure project to date. Prometheus, our gigawatt-scale supercluster, is an advancement in our infrastructure that is training the next generation of foundational models that will bring new AI experiences to billions of people. Two years ago, New Albany was a conventional data center site running web traffic. With advancements in hardware, networking and building design, we reworked this site to be home to training programs for frontier models. We’re building the supercluster in phases. The first phase has already been completed and was used to train our Muse foundational models , including the Muse Wonder models, our new frontier models that deliver state-of-the-art performance on personal and professional agentic tasks. Large training jobs require everything to work optimally to sustain their performance; an issue on a single host can slow down or stop the entire job, lowering its ‘goodput’. By focusing on improving our systems’ stability and reliability we were able to achieve more than 85% goodput for pre-training runs and more than 90% goodput for reinforcement learning (RL) runs of Muse Wonder. During these training runs, we were able to achieve an overall wall-clock mean time between interruptions (MTBI) of ~47k GPU hours. Since then, we have landed further changes across our fleet including firmware fixes to increase MTBI to more than 54K GPU hours, and we are constantly improving it. Now, we’re continuing to scale Prometheus with our next frontier models from Meta Superintelligence Labs in mind. https://engineering.fb.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/AIM-1210-Superclusters_Video_v1.mp4 The Prometheus supercluster is housed in Meta’s New Albany, Ohio, data center. The Supercluster: Unlocking New AI Capabilities Today, Prometheus comprises an array of hundreds of thousands of GPUs across multiple interconnected buildings, including traditional and AI-optimized data center buildings and rapid deployment structures, all tightly interconnected by miles of fiber and functioning as a single machine. This capacity allows us to pursue larger models and longer context windows than were previously practical. At full scale, Prometheus will comprise roughly 1 million distributed GPUs, all functioning in lockstep. Multiple Generations of AI Hardware Prometheus currently deploys two NVIDIA GPU platforms, with a third (based on NVIDIA’s Vera Rubin NVL72 ) arriving soon. Each represents a generational leap in performance and efficiency, leveraging our NVL72 rack architecture where 72 GPUs act as a single accelerator within the same network fabric. Catalina: NVIDIA GB200 Our first platform, Catalina , leverages the NVIDIA GB200 NVL72. We deploy the Ariel variant, a two-rack configuration in which 36 GPUs per rack are interconnected via NVLink to form a unified 72-GPU domain. Catalina provides improvements in raw compute and memory capacity compared to Grand Teton H100 . title: Beyond the patch: Protecting your NetScaler gateway against future vulnerabilities
excerpt: The recent disclosure of a major vulnerability in Citrix NetScaler pointed to a widespread weak point: a login page is an attack surface that can be used to compromise and access an application server. Indeed, the disclosures included an actively exploited flaw that allowed attackers to execute commands on affected gateways without signing in. As with any emergency patch, admins had to weigh cutting off or disrupting their users’ access with the risk of delaying a critical security update. If you’re a NetScaler customer and you haven’t patched your instance, stop reading and go do that. This was a bad one. Once you’ve finished the patch, we’ll explore how to avoid a future fire drill by laying additional security controls. This issue extends beyond NetScaler and can be applied to any internal application available on the Internet. Remote desktop portals, administrative consoles, and other publicly accessible authentication pages all deserve the same scrutiny: Does the intended audience require unrestricted Internet reachability? And can an attacker bypass this authentication check to reach the application's server? Citrix released software updates to address the flaw , and Cloudflare followed with an emergency web application firewall (WAF) rule on October 1. But having a patch available does not guarantee safety: every instance has to be identified, updated, and tested. Applying updates across a production deployment is painful — it can result in downtime or cause disruptions to employees who still need their desktops throughout that process. Customers, patients, and others dependent on users of a remote desktop definitely don’t care about your security patch. Using a web application firewall (WAF) can buy some additional time before a patch can be fully rolled out, but it’s reactive and does not account for the next exploit that’s discovered. Cloudflare and other security vendors do their best to cover variations and similar attacks. But AI is hastening how rapidly attackers can discover new and novel variants. That’s why it is crucial to build defense in depth , to ensure that no specific software failure or exploit will lead to a critical security issue. Cloudflare combines access policies, web application security, and restricted origin connections to protect the authentication service before a new vulnerability is disclosed. Access controls limit who can reach the application server; WAF inspection evaluates web requests for attacks; origin restrictions prevent direct connections from bypassing those defenses. These reduce exposure without waiting for a new exploit signature or replacing the existing desktop platform. The NetScaler exploit Citrix's September 27, 2026 bulletin reported observed exploitation of CVE-2026-88771 and CVE-2026-88772. The first allows unauthenticated command execution on affected appliances, including in their default configuration. The second affects configurations using Datagram Transport Layer Security, or DTLS. Further advisories on October 3 and October 8 addressed additional vulnerabilities in SAML configurations. These exploits allowed attackers to execute arbitrary scripts on target machines and also execute denial of service attacks. CISA's alert and Mandiant's technical investigation cover the vulnerabilities, observed exploitation, and response guidance in more detail. For details of the available web application protection, see Cloudflare's emergency WAF release for CVE-2026-88771 . In a typical Citrix deployment, the user authenticates through NetScaler Gateway, which then uses a secure ticket authority to pass through to the StoreFront, which presents the applications and desktops available to that user. The native-installed Citrix app then uses that information to establish a separate connection using Citrix's Independent Computing Architecture (ICA) protocol. title: Cutting our inference bill by 68% by being obsessive about optimization
excerpt: When we previously blogged about our AI code reviewer in April , an average review cost a palatable $1.19. By the end of August, that figure had shot up to about $2.46. We hadn't made any significant architectural changes: the coordinator was still handing work to the same set of specialist reviewers, and the same risk tiers decided how intensive of a review we gave. Around mid-September we tasked our agents with working out where those tokens were going and cutting them — aggressively. With code quality at high effort, the average review now costs just $0.77, down 68% from the $2.43 it averaged over our two most expensive weeks before we started. Our main goal was to cut costs, but as part of this work we also managed to optimize the reviewer, so that the median review now takes just 1m 32s instead of the 4m 09s it took before. About 40% of the savings came from changes and optimizations to the reviewer's code, and the rest from experimenting with which models we use and how much effort they put in. How a review doubled in cost The chart below shows the cost of an average review on each weekday since March. It holds the mix of review tiers fixed, so a day with more large reviews doesn't skew the data. The cost per review steadily rose from $1.22 (March) → $1.44 (June) → $1.74 (July) and finally, to $2.32 (August). A small part of that is that more reviews landed in the most expensive tier (59% of reviews in March and then 65% in August). We believe there’s a simple answer for why: models are getting much better, and much more capable. Naturally, engineers are producing bigger, more complex changes which means more of them fall into our “full review” tier. We found that most of the cost increase actually came from model changes over those months, though. At the start of August we moved every reviewer onto Anthropic models, which raised the cost per job from $1.38 to $2.03. We made this choice because we found that during our evals, Anthropic models performed better on this specific workload than other models. Our internal standards reviewer, Codex , ended up on Claude Opus 4.7 due to a mix of performance and reliability. That took it from about $0.25 per review to $0.88 in August, which made it more expensive than the coordinator agent itself. The cache hit rate also increased, going from 85.7% in April to 97% by September, while the number of tokens per review more than tripled, from 0.91 million to 2.99 million. A high hit rate on three times as many tokens still costs a lot more, even with the low cache read cost. What else has changed since our last post? One of the biggest changes is that the reviewer now runs on OpenCode v2, which is a ground-up rewrite from v1. Before switching all reviews over from v1 to v2, we ran every review in every canary repo on both v1 and v2 in a comparative shadow mode. The two agreed on the approval decision in 98% of the merge requests we tested, so we moved everyone over in one go in early October and removed the v1 code. Comparing two days with the same models, full-tier reviews on v2 finish about 13% faster. We’re also currently experimenting with other ways to run our internal AI reviewer, including solely on Durable Objects using pi-durable . We’re hopefully going to have more on this coming soon, so keep an eye out! So, where were the tokens going? Right before we started focusing on cost optimization, our AI review spend was split by: output tokens making up about 23%, cache writes cost 43%, and cache reads cost 34%. This means that most of the money was going on context the model had already seen or was about to see again. That makes complete sense when you look into a single session. The code quality reviewer made 16.6 large language model (LLM) calls per review on average and over those calls it wrote 72k tokens to the cache and read back 1.08m, because each call sends the whole conversation as context. title: Introducing Clairic, a new System One class of extraction models
excerpt: Today, we're announcing a preview of a new class of System One-style models: extraction models. Our first one, Clairic, is available hosted on Workers AI as @cf/cloudflare/clairic. We intend to release the model open-weights soon. Clairic is an extraction model that is able to extract, compute, estimate, and forecast values from unstructured inputs — all at a significantly higher accuracy, faster latency, and cheaper cost than traditional LLMs. Context When System One models were announced by TypeSafe a month ago, it took the industry by storm. As referenced by TypeSafe in their blog and defined by Daniel Kahneman’s book Thinking, Fast and Slow , a System One model should be fast and precise, which contrasts a System Two model that is capable of deliberate reasoning (like LLMs). With this, TypeSafe introduced Jev — a model that is purpose-fit for a specific use case, and priced accessibly given its niche domain. It excelled where LLMs failed, helping users make decisions based on probabilities and well-typed outputs. The introduction of Jev prompted people to start thinking about a new class of models that were not LLMs and how to integrate them into their workflows. We were inspired by the concept of System One models and started thinking about other tasks where LLMs are inefficient. There are many structured-output calls going to frontier LLMs today with the same shapes again and again: What's the invoice total? When was this delivered? How many days late is it? What will this repair cost? What will traffic look like over the next 24 hours? None of these have answers you can list out in advance, which is needed for a decision model to give probabilities against. That led us to the class of models we're introducing today: System One extraction models. Introducing System One extraction models Until now, every System One model has been a decision model: Jev and Clef take an input state and a list of questions and give probabilities against the inputs and your listed questions. Clairic is the first model in a new class: System One extraction models. It is still fast, typed, and cheap, but it answers with values directly extracted from the input, computed from it, or predicted beyond it. Most model tasks ask for one of three kinds of output: a number, a choice from a fixed set, or open-ended text. Clairic handles the first, returning numbers with an 80% range, and also pulls typed values like names, dates and lists out of the input. Clef handles the second: it picks among options and returns a probability for each. LLMs handle the third. We call Clairic and Clef System One models because they answer in a single pass, without reasoning or generating tokens. They charge only for input and typically respond in under a second, while an LLM that reasons through the same step takes several seconds. An extraction model can return: Extracted values: Text copied from the input, such as a name, an order ID or a description. Each one comes back as a span with its character offsets and a confidence score. Including, computed values: Numbers, dates, times, datetimes, durations and lists, read from the input or worked out from it. They follow the rules of their type (for example, two decimals for cents) and come with a confidence score. Estimated values: Values the input doesn't state but gives evidence for. Each one comes back as a distribution inside the bounds you declare, on the grid you specify, with a median and an 80% interval. Forecasted values: Future values of a series, one estimate per step ahead, each with its own 80% interval. And because it generates no tokens, it can't produce a mistyped answer or “hallucinate” in the same way as an LLM (though it can, of course, make mistakes). Outputs are a value of the type you asked for, or null when the model fails to find an answer in the input. It also comes with confidence scores against the outputs to help you evaluate if it is appropriate to trust the model or to take a second look. He

title: AWS Weekly Roundup: AWS Lambda Web Functions, Amazon S3 on the Vercel Marketplace, and more (October 19, 2026)
excerpt: Nothing last week added a new kind of compute. What it did instead was shorten the distance between the code you already have and that code being live. AWS Lambda learned to run a plain HTTP server with no adapter in front of it, and Amazon S3 became something you can provision from inside the tool you were already using, without opening the AWS Management Console. Different services, same direction. The counterweight arrived on Thursday. As it gets easier to put things into production, it matters more that you can say what those things are allowed to do, and this week’s most interesting read is about exactly that. Now, let’s get into this week’s AWS news… Headlines AWS Lambda Web Functions is a new form factor that runs a standard HTTP web application on Lambda without rewriting it into an event handler. You take a port-listening server built with Express, Hono, Fastify, or Next.js, run aws lambda-web deploy , and get back a live HTTPS URL in under a minute. No adapters, no infrastructure to set up first, no framework lock-in. Lambda now has three form factors on the same Firecracker isolation, which compose inside one application: Event Functions (the model you already know) for async work, Web Functions for the user-facing layer, and MicroVMs for stateful sandboxes running untrusted code. Two details make this more than repackaging. Each execution environment handles up to 128 concurrent requests, so a burst of traffic shares warm environments instead of mapping one request to one environment, and billing meters the CPU time your code actually uses rather than wall-clock time. For server-side rendering, API backends, and inference endpoints streaming tokens, where most of the elapsed time is spent waiting, that changes the arithmetic. Adding --regions to the same deploy command replicates your code and configures latency-based routing behind a single global URL, and you can split traffic across revisions by weight for a canary rollout. It’s available in five Regions, running Node.js 24 on Arm64 with VPC connectivity. The AWS Compute Blog has a longer walkthrough, and Amazon CloudFront can now use a Web Function endpoint as an origin with origin access control. The week’s other headline isn’t a launch. Trust in Depth: giving agents more autonomy without losing control makes an argument I keep running into in practice: putting a person in the loop for every agent action works at small scale and then quietly stops working, because people asked to check everything stop catching what matters. The alternative is four questions answered at four moments, which AWS calls scope, know, bound, and observe. The part worth sitting with is that an agent’s limits belong outside its own reasoning, in Amazon Bedrock AgentCore policies enforced at the gateway, because an agent cannot turn off a control it does not run. AWS has run automated reasoning in production for more than a decade, including AWS Identity and Access Management at more than 2.1 billion requests per second, and the case here is for pointing it at the rules you write for agents. Last week’s launches Here are some launches and updates from this past week that caught my attention: Amazon S3 is now available on the Vercel Marketplace and v0 by Vercel – You can now provision S3 general purpose buckets, S3 Tables , and S3 Vectors from the Vercel dashboard, or by describing what you want to build in v0. It joins existing integrations for Amazon Aurora , Amazon DynamoDB , and Amazon OpenSearch Serverless , so the whole stack sits in one AWS account with one bill. The authentication detail is the good part: a short-lived OIDC token is exchanged at runtime with AWS Security Token Service for credentials scoped to that resource, so no static keys are stored anywhere. title: AI Gateway logs now show session affinity
excerpt: AI Gateway logs now have a Sessions view that groups requests into sessions and shows how session affinity routed each one. Each row shows the coding agent or app that ran the session, such as Claude Code, Codex, or Cursor, along with its cost, models, providers, and how much of its input was cached across every turn. Open a session to see its cache hit rate, duration, and path. The path lists each turn with its model and timing, and names the provider serving the session along with any earlier ones. Session affinity sends each turn to the provider that served the one before it, so the provider already has most of the prompt in cache. A session that stays on one provider reads more of each prompt from cache . Filter sessions by turns, client, model, provider, authentication, or cost. Single-turn sessions are hidden until you clear the minimum turns filter. Session affinity runs by default on text and chat requests. To group requests yourself, send the same sessionId in providerOptions.gateway , or the same x-session-id header, on every request in a conversation. Requests without one are grouped by a fingerprint of the conversation's opening and appear as fingerprinted sessions. Read the session affinity documentation for more information on how AI Gateway identifies sessions. Read more

title: Vercel and Shopify make agents first-class shoppers
excerpt: Agents already shop on the web, but they often use pages and tools originally built for people and search engines. Building a better shopping experience for agents means treating them as first-class shoppers, with product information they can read directly and tools designed for agents to shop. Today, Vercel Shop , our open source Next.js storefront template for Shopify , is generally available. Teams can launch storefronts optimized for how people, search engines, and agents interact with them. Vercel Shop is built on Shopify’s Hydrogen SDK . The SDK gives teams access to the store’s product catalog, cart and order management, payments, and checkout to build custom storefronts. Earlier this year, Vercel and Shopify announced plans to rebuild Hydrogen to work across JavaScript frameworks. Today, the rebuilt SDK is generally available . Give agents the information and tools they need Vercel Shop makes product pages available as machine-readable content , including price, availability, and options. The same product URL can serve a visual page to people or product information that agents can read without interpreting the page’s layout. The template also includes structured data embedded in pages and sitemaps to help search and answer engines discover and understand the products. Shopify co-developed the Universal Commerce Protocol (UCP), which gives agents a standard way to search a store’s catalog, read product details, check availability, build a cart, and get a checkout link. Vercel Shop makes these capabilities discoverable at the merchant’s own domain, so agents can use MCP to search products and build carts without navigating the site. Customize the experience for all customers Vercel Shop brings the store’s product catalog, cart, and checkout together with a Next.js storefront, product information and shopping tools for agents, and a shopping assistant powered by eve . The storefront and assistant live in the same codebase, so teams can customize the store’s design and how the assistant helps shoppers. Skills included in the template guide coding agents through setup, customization, and template updates. Teams can create an experience where shoppers browse product pages or ask the assistant to find products and add them to their cart. Both share the same cart, so shoppers keep what they’ve added as they move between experiences. Storefronts built with Shopify and Vercel Today, we launched our merch store at vercel.store with limited-edition drops. It’s built on Vercel Shop. The store’s shopping agent helps shoppers find products, add them to their cart, and continue to checkout. Shopify, Next.js, and Vercel already power storefronts for brands including AG1, Bombas, and PAIGE. When PAIGE re-architected its ecommerce platform , it saw a 22% increase in revenue and a 76% increase in conversion over Black Friday and Cyber Monday, with no downtime. title: Ontology-Driven Observability: Building an End-to-End Knowledge Graph at Netflix Scale
excerpt: Prasanna Vijayanathan , Renzo Sanchez-Silva When Jake Paul and Mike Tyson stepped into the ring in November 2024, we delivered the fight to roughly 65 million concurrent streams. On an ordinary day our infrastructure takes in more than 2 billion requests and handles upwards of 38 million real-time logging events every second. At that scale, the whole picture doesn’t fit into a single engineering team’s head or onto a single dashboard. With more Live content, Podcasts and real-time streams, our need to understand and update our systems as quickly as possible becomes imperative to provide a good user experience. Understanding the system at this scale and within the time constraints we have, often becomes a daunting exercise in finding a needle in a haystack, in a dark jungle, blindfolded. This post is about that search for the needle. The Four hours before a fix Consider a regression of the kind we see in a given week. The home screen where you see the list of lists of movies, starts taking about 1.5 seconds longer to render. An alert fires. And then we go looking for what caused this issue and how do we fix it? As it so happens, a regression on the application could be related to anywhere in the system — a client app regression from a new version deployment or A/B test rollout, a load shedding in the infrastructure, a GraphQL query responding with bad data because of a service rollout 6 hops downstream, are all suspects at this point. So, answering “what caused the issue?” needs insights from across the system, and this involves combing through layers of data in a meticulous manner. The MELT Layer “What caused the issue?” Metrics, events, logs and traces, or MELT, in the industry’s shorthand, are the right raw materials for such an investigation, and each of them answers roughly a quarter of the question. We collect observability data across these four pillars, unified into a single observability data layer. This lets us observe our systems in real time, across what our users are experiencing, how our applications are doing and what our backend infrastructure and services are processing and responding to. MELT — Metrics, Events, Logs and Traces, and how they are captured across the system. The investigation that follows may look like this in each layer: What each layer of MELT tells us and what it leaves out The timeline of an investigation So how long does it take to investigate an issue, figure out the root cause and fix it, so our users stop running into this issue again? A timeline of an investigation: ~4 hours In our chosen example, four hours. Very little of it went into computing anything difficult. Most of it went into reconstructing relationships that our observability systems already knew but we had never written down anywhere a human or machine could simply read and discover. The disagreement underneath The instinct here could have been, around 2023, to reach for more data or better dashboards, and while both help at the margins, neither addresses what makes these investigations slow. It’s 2026 now, so we might say, “hey, agents”, but without the right context delivered to the agents, AI systems hallucinate, and especially when teams are on-call and need a fix “now”, we cannot let inaccurate agentic analysis lead us down the wrong path. We need the right needle, not any needle. Each of our systems is internally coherent and externally isolated. Atlas , our telemetry platform, knows applications and their time series. Radar, our alerting system, knows thresholds and firing history. incident.io knows severities and responders. PagerDuty knows rotations. Spinnaker knows what shipped and when. And our Slack history knows, in a form no query engine can reach, which engineer solved something very similar last quarter and what they found. title: Continuous accountability for Verified bots
excerpt: A driver’s license tells you who someone is and that they passed a driving test, not whether they’ll drive responsibly in the future. The same is true for bots: verifying who operates it creates accountability, but trust depends on what it does next. A known bot can still ignore website preferences, overwhelm origins, or evade controls. It’s not always malicious — often it’s just a misconfiguration or a bug. As we described in a previous blog post on bot behavior, we strive to verify two questions: “Are you who you say you are?” and “Can we trust you?” To be a Cloudflare Verified Bot, you broadly need to meet three criteria: Identify yourself accurately and securely Do only what you say you will do Don’t engage in abusive behavior Bots use Web Bot Auth to sign requests that establish their identity, which BotBase then catalogues in an open format. With identification addressed, our focus shifts to the second cardinal rule of Verified bots: thou shalt do no harm . Today we introduce a system to evaluate and report when Verified bot behavior starts to deviate from this rule, ensuring that the answer to “Can we trust you?” remains “Yes.” This is where the distinction between risk and trust becomes important: Risk describes the likelihood that a particular request or point-in-time action may be harmful, and it can change from one moment to the next. Trust is built over time through repeated and consistent behavior. For example, we de-listed Perplexity’s bot from our Verified bot list in 2025 when it sought to access resources on websites that opted out of scraping and subsequently attempted to circumvent controls when those requests were blocked. Do not engage in abusive behavior This simple requirement sounds like a freebie, but there is a lot of nuance in that statement. When crawlers don’t respect site preferences , that undermines trust. When sites request a crawler to not crawl or to slow down, and the crawler ignores these requests, that undermines trust. We developed a system to measure how often a crawler respects site preferences. These observations will translate to an explainable trust band: a range showing how consistently a bot respects site preferences and which observed behaviors informed that assessment, rather than a permanent judgment about a bot or its operator. The initial signals we evaluate are: Does the bot respect instructions? Did it respond to direct feedback? We consider these to be “common sense” rules, a courtesy to the operators who provide the information bots seek. In the future, we will be sharing these scores publicly on Radar , as well as expanding the ways we measure. This score gives responsible bot operators a way to demonstrate that trust is being upheld over time. Verify, but continuously re-verify. When in Rome, do as the Romans do A robots.txt file is the primary way to communicate site owner preferences. Our system considers whether a bot’s observed traffic is consistent with those published preferences over time. Robots.txt tells all (or specific) bots to only crawl specific parts of a website. Isolated violations and other types of one-offs may not be significant. What we look for instead are repeated patterns of behavior that disregards site preferences. The expectation is simply for responsible bots to consult and honor the preferences that websites publish, in line with RFC 9309 . And just to be clear, a robots.txt sets the minimum rules for what bots and agents should not do. But there is no implication that anything not stated is allowed. For example, a robots.txt does not need to say that a bot must stop when the site can communicate that continued access is unwelcome through other signals. What you do not wish for yourself, do not impose on others Bots can remain entirely within allowed paths while still placing substantial load on the websites they visit. title: Vercel Drives is now generally available
excerpt: Vercel Drives is now generally available for Vercel Sandbox on Hobby, Pro, and Enterprise. A Drive is persistent storage that you mount as a directory in a Vercel Sandbox. Its files remain available after the sandbox stops, so later runs and other sandboxes can access them by mounting the same Drive. Use Drives to preserve an agent’s workspace or file-based memory across runs, or to make datasets, models, dependencies, and build artifacts available across sandboxes. You can also fork a Drive into independent writable Drives. Forks inherit the source Drive's data, region, and maximum size, then store their own changes. Parallel workers can start with the same files and make changes without affecting the original or one another. Learn more in the Drives documentation . Read more

title: Vercel Daemons is now in public beta
excerpt: Vercel Daemons is now in public beta, allowing you to run long-running processes that pull and execute work from Vercel Queues , databases, or third-party systems without requiring an HTTP server: Consumers using Vercel Queues poll mode , Celery, BullMQ, RabbitMQ, or Kafka. Temporal or Cadence workers that long-poll their task queues. Self-hosted CI runners for GitHub Actions, GitLab, or CircleCI that poll for jobs without requiring inbound connections. Daemons run containers on Fluid compute and deploy alongside your app in the same project. Vercel builds your image and maintains the instance count you configure in each region, restarting instances that exit or crash. Get started by packaging your application and dependencies in a Dockerfile or Containerfile, then adding a daemons entry to one configuration file at your project root. This example uses worker/Dockerfile to run one Celery worker in iad1 (Washington, D.C.): Set any connection details your worker needs in your project's production environment variables, then deploy to production. Vercel starts the configured instances, and their output appears in your project's Logs . CPU and memory metrics are available with Observability Plus . Learn more in the Vercel Daemons documentation and read the complete guide . Read more

title: Vercel Connect now supports Secure Compute
excerpt: Vercel Connect now supports Secure Compute , allowing connectors to reach providers with IP allowlists, such as Salesforce and Snowflake. With Secure Compute routing enabled, Connect’s provider requests use the selected network’s dedicated static IP addresses instead of Connect’s shared IPs. Requests to obtain and refresh access tokens follow that route; your app’s direct API routing is unchanged by this setting. Credential management stays the same, so you don’t need to store long-lived provider secrets in your app or build OAuth flows yourself. To enable Secure Compute routing for a supported connector and all projects that use it: Open your connector’s Settings in the Vercel dashboard. Under Secure Compute Routing , choose an existing network. If your provider uses an IP allowlist, add the selected network’s displayed IP addresses to it in the provider’s settings. Save your changes in Connect. Requests for initial connector creation and all provider discovery requests bypass the selected network and connect directly to providers. If the selected network is unavailable, routed requests fail instead of falling back to Connect’s shared IPs. Read the Secure Compute routing documentation for configuration details. Read more

excerpt: For a decade, Vercel has shaped how the web is built. Now, we’re doing the same for agents. Agentic infrastructure Guillermo Rauch (CEO, Vercel) opened Ship SF with a vision for the next era of software and agentic infrastructure: interfaces generated for any task in front of you, agents that reproduce and fix bugs autonomously, and software that takes production context and continuously improves itself. Agentic infrastructure has three parts: Vercel is where you build and deploy your own apps and agents . We give you every tool you need to build and run apps and agents in production, securely, at scale. Vercel is where coding agents deploy that software . When you ask your harness where to deploy, you get Vercel, because Vercel is built for the way agents work. We have over 200 CLI commands that your agent can use to operate our entire platform. Vercel itself is automated by agents . Vercel runs your apps in production, handling traffic, traces, observability, and anomalies. That data gives our agents the context they need to investigate autonomously, and then surface pull requests, not just alerts. Agentic Infrastructure is for developers In his opening keynote, Guillermo pointed to claims that AI would replace developers, then used Vercel's own data to prove them wrong. In the last 12 months: The number of developers on Vercel has grown 3x The number of new projects developers ship has doubled The number of their agent-triggered deployments has increased 28x "We built Vercel for developers," he said, "because they are the difference between a world full of slop and a world full of software worth using." The Agent Stack gives you everything you need to build, run, and scale agents in production. Vercel Drives , now generally available for Sandbox, gives agents persistent workspaces. Code, data, and saved memory survive across runs, so you can change runtimes or compute without rebuilding the workspace. eve , our open-source framework for building agents, now has persistent memory across sessions, extensions for installing tools and skills, and agent creation and deployment from the Vercel dashboard. title: Vercel for Enterprise
excerpt: AI adoption in the enterprise is growing rapidly, and expanding beyond engineering users. In the last three months, token usage by enterprise companies on AI Gateway has quadrupled, and OpenAI recently reported that from August 2025 to June 2026, non-developer Codex users grew 189x. Our customers call these builders citizen developers. They know their part of the business better than anyone else, and with AI they can create the software they need to ship work faster and deliver better customer experiences. Building has never been easier, but that also means that control and governance have never been harder. Employees are using AI tools whether they are approved or not , and if a citizen developer vibe codes a login page incorrectly, private data can reach the public internet. Enterprise leaders have to figure out how to let everyone build, without giving up security or control. Enterprise Apps and Agents We built Enterprise Apps and Agents to solve these challenges at Vercel, and in June, we made it available to our customers. Enterprise Apps and Agents is a central control plane for governing every builder, app, agent, token, and dollar. Today, we are expanding the platform: Bring Your Own Cloud (BYOC) on AWS is generally available, giving you the full Vercel developer experience, while keeping compute and data inside your AWS boundary. Enterprise-Managed Authorization through Vercel Connect is launching in public beta, giving agents the ability to access connected services on behalf of employees through your IdP. A single control plane for governing enterprise AI Enterprise Apps and Agents gives you a single deployment destination for both engineers and citizen developers, with central governance over access, providers, models, data retention, token budgets, integrations, and policies, managed through your existing IdP. Vercel centralizes AI governance so that company policies can be applied consistently across control domains. Control domain Vercel controls Deployment governance Enterprise Managed Users and RBAC Access governance Vercel Passport , Deployment Protection , and Vercel Firewall Integration and data governance Vercel Connect and Enterprise-Managed Authorization Model and token governance AI Gateway , including US-only inference and budget controls Apps and agents run on the same infrastructure that powers billions of production deployments, and Vercel gives you a single place for observability and security monitoring across every project, through analytics , audit logs , and the Security Dashboard . Secure Compute provides private connectivity to enterprise systems, while BYOC on AWS lets your application functions run in your own AWS account under your permissions and network controls. Deployment governance Citizen developers and engineers use different tools. A marketer might use ChatGPT to build a landing page, an analyst might use Claude Code to run queries and build a report, and an engineer might use Codex, OpenCode, or fx. No matter the harness, Vercel gives you a single deployment target, and connects to your existing IdP, so you can control who creates deployments. How Klaviyo's built a secure internal app platform Before Vercel, shipping a simple internal app at Klaviyo took two weeks of chasing IT, opening tickets for engineering, and following up with the platform team. They built an internal app-building platform on top of Enterprise Apps and Agents, and now anyone in the company can deploy an idea in three minutes. In their first two weeks on Vercel, 512 employees deployed 356 apps. Access governance Controlling who can deploy doesn't protect the apps, agents, and data that make it into production. On Vercel, you can configure every deployment to be private by default, and with Vercel Passport, you can require employees to authenticate through your IdP before they can access internal apps. title: Python on Vercel is now generally available
excerpt: Python on Vercel is now generally available. Build and run Python applications with the frameworks, libraries, and tools you already use. Vercel automatically detects supported frameworks and configures the build and deployment. Your applications run on Fluid compute, which manages concurrent requests and scales with traffic. Idiomatic Python SDKs let you work with storage, queues, durable workflows, and AI models directly from Python. For full-stack projects, the Python backend and frontend share a workflow for local development, preview deployments, and production releases. Our goals for Python on Vercel Ten months ago, we set out to make Vercel the best place to build and run Python applications . We wanted the experience to fit how Python developers already work, with three goals guiding our decisions: Idiomatic Python SDKs. Working with Vercel infrastructure should feel familiar to Python developers, with APIs that use type annotations, async / await , and context managers. A shared workflow for both the frontend and backend. Python applications often include a JavaScript frontend, so developers should be able to run both locally, review them in the same preview deployment, and release or roll them back together. Compatibility with the Python ecosystem. The runtime should use CPython, the standard Python interpreter, on Linux to preserve compatibility with the packages and tools Python developers already rely on. The first test of those goals is what happens when you deploy a Python application on Vercel: its framework, dependencies, and project structure should guide how it’s built and run. Deploying Python applications on Vercel We’ve worked to make Python feel native on Vercel. Vercel reads your project’s dependency files, including those managed by uv , and automatically detects frameworks such as FastAPI, Flask, Django, and FastHTML. Framework defined infrastructure configures builds and request routing, with framework-specific support for serving static assets through the CDN. For applications with a frontend, Vercel Services brings both parts into one project. Running vercel dev starts them together, and shared previews let you test backend changes with the frontend that uses them. For long-running workers that pull jobs from queues or databases, Vercel Daemons keeps your containers running with your Python code along with any of its packages, and system dependencies. Python SDKs for Vercel infrastructure A Python backend might need to store files, send messages, run durable workflows, or call AI models. We’ve built Python SDKs for these tasks, with APIs that follow the conventions of the language: These SDKs work alongside your framework and libraries, and the example below shows how they connect within a full-stack application. Start building with Python on Vercel Whether you’re starting a new project or deploying existing code, the framework guides cover setup and deployment on Vercel. For a guided full-stack project, the Python on Vercel course walks through building a FastAPI backend and Next.js frontend, then deploying them together with Services. To show how these pieces work together, I built a collaborative web application to create and browse Python notebooks. It lets people create their own notebooks, publish them for others to browse or fork, and work with an AI assistant to write and run Python code. The application pairs a Vite frontend with a FastAPI backend and uses PostgreSQL for notebook source and chat history. Services keeps the frontend and backend in one deployment, with the frontend served through the CDN. Here’s how the main parts connect: Editing and running code: When a signed-in user opens their notebook in the editor, FastAPI creates or reuses a Vercel Sandbox running Jupyter, keeping user code isolated from the application backend. title: Introducing Vercel Drives: persistent storage for agents
excerpt: Agents often handle complex work that continues across runs. As that work evolves, they may need a new environment with different tools, runtimes, or compute. They should be able to continue working with the same files when they change environments. We built Vercel Drives to keep an agent’s files independent of its execution environment. It is now generally available for Vercel Sandbox . Agents can mount the same drive in a new environment configured for the next task and continue where they left off. Persisting state with a drive Create a drive once, then mount it when you create a sandbox. From the CLI: Or from the Sandbox SDK: In this example, everything under /workspace persists on the drive. Everything else belongs to the sandbox. The next sandbox that mounts the drive finds the repository, and anything else the agent wrote there, where the previous run left it. The drive keeps the agent’s files independent of the sandbox running it. An agent can resume work in a new sandbox or switch runtimes without transferring its workspace. Other sandboxes can mount the same drive. Sharing state across sandboxes Agents can prepare files on a drive once and reuse them across sandboxes. If one agent builds a dataset on a drive, other agents can mount read-only copies to analyze the data or generate reports without rebuilding the dataset. They use the shared files as input and save their results separately. Agents can also fork a drive to explore different approaches independently. Each fork starts with the drive’s contents and provides its own writable workspace. Agents can try different transformations of the dataset in parallel without changing the original or affecting one another. Forks don’t merge back into the original drive. Forking is generally available . Get started Vercel Drives is now generally available for Vercel Sandbox on all plans. Drives default to 1 TiB, or 1 GiB on Hobby, with up to 16 TiB available. See the documentation for configuration, snapshots, and limits, or the changelog for what changed at GA. Frameworks such as FastAPI, Flask, and Django run on standard CPython with your PyPI dependencies, while Vercel handles framework detection, builds, and scaling. With ten engineers and no dedicated infrastructure role, the team ships to production more than 100 times a day and uses Queues to handle background jobs. Applications in any language with containers The Vercel container runtime lets you deploy applications written in any language, packaged with the OS libraries and executables they need. Since container support entered Public Beta, 5,000 teams have shipped 150,000 container deployments on Vercel. Containers deploy as Vercel Functions on Fluid compute, scaling with traffic and using Active CPU pricing , which doesn’t charge for idle time spent waiting for API responses, database queries, or LLM inferencing.
